sections.html:
Property tax in Owen County runs through three offices in Owenton. One collects the money, one decides the value, and one keeps the records once a bill goes unpaid or an appeal is filed.

Owen County offices involved in property tax
OfficeJobContact
SheriffTakes in state, county and school district tax103 W. Perry St.; 502-484-3363; Mon-Fri 8 a.m.-4 p.m.
Property Valuation AdministrationSets values and fields bill questions502-484-5172
County ClerkDelinquent tax listings, deeds, liens136 W. Bryan St.; 502-484-2213; Mon-Fri 8 a.m.-4:30 p.m., lunch closure noon to 1

The sheriff assigns no values, so a dispute over the amount begins with the PVA, not at the collection counter.

Owen County covers about 354 square miles of northern Kentucky, with Owenton as the seat and Glencoe and Gratz as the only other cities. It is thinly settled, at 32.1 residents per square mile in 2020, and the entire population lived in rural areas at the last census. The count was 11,278 in 2020, with an estimate of 11,601 for mid-2025.

  • Homes owned by their occupants have a median value of $168,700, and 88.0 percent of the 4,252 households own.
  • Mortgage holders spend $1,385 a month at the median, and renters pay $830.
  • The typical household earns $61,134.
  • Getting to work takes 41.9 minutes on average, a long drive that shapes who buys here.
  • Only 17 building permits were issued in 2025.

Of 5,323 housing units in 2020, 18.3 percent stood vacant, a high share that includes seasonal and unsold property. Expect a quiet market in which many sales are older houses and land.

sections.h2: Payment dates for an Owen County bill
sections.html:
Sheriffs across Kentucky use the schedule in KRS 134.015. Owen County residents get a 2 percent break for paying by November 1, owe the stated amount until year end, and add 5 percent in January, then 10 percent from February.

April 15 ends the sheriff's collection season. What remains unpaid turns into a certificate of delinquency at the County Clerk, with a lien noted against the parcel.

If you are selling in the middle of the year, remember that the owner on January 1 is the one billed. Ask the title agent to prorate the year between you and the buyer, and keep your receipt.

sections.h2: Planning your visit to the PVA
sections.html:
Call 502-484-5172 before you drive over. Tell the office what you want to discuss, whether it is a value, an exemption or the mailing address on a bill, and ask what to bring. Bring your latest bill, and for an appeal add the evidence described below.

Photos that show a leaking roof, a failing septic system or an old furnace are worth more than a general complaint. So are quotes from contractors and the sale prices of houses close to yours. If you own acreage, be ready to describe the land and any outbuildings.

Begin with a talk at the PVA office. Arrive with your own value figure and proof, such as nearby sales, an appraisal, damage photos or contractor quotes. Landlords add rent and expense records.

  1. Talk to the PVA while the roll is open for inspection each spring.
  2. Collect the appeal form from the clerk at 136 W. Bryan Street and return it by the next business day after inspection ends.
  3. Present your evidence to a local board of three residents.
  4. If the ruling stands and you disagree, send the state Board of Tax Appeals a letter within a month of the notice.

You may pay on your own claimed value while an appeal is pending, but a higher final figure produces a supplemental bill.

The clerk's website posts the delinquent list along with investor registration forms. The state revenue department sets a normal-schedule sale between July 14 and August 28, no sooner than 90 days after the bills reach the clerk.

  • Each month adds 1 percent interest.
  • The county attorney sends two letters, and the second names the sale date.
  • Newspaper notices run roughly a month to six weeks before the sale.
  • A certificate that sells to an investor can carry added fees.

If you are selling a listed parcel, ask the clerk (502-484-2213) for a written payoff. The title company will use it to pay the balance from your proceeds, which is usually simpler than letting the debt reach an investor.

Homeowners who are 65 or older or totally disabled can shelter part of a home's assessed value through the homestead exemption. The state sets the amount and reviews it every two years. An owner with a total service-connected disability applies once, but a buyer starts fresh.

Working farm acreage is assessed at agricultural value, not market value, which can cut the taxable amount sharply. Before a farm is sold or split, ask the PVA whether the tract qualifies.

The transfer tax is the seller's: half a dollar per $500 of value, with any partial block counted whole (KRS 142.050). The clerk wants proof of payment before taking the deed.

The deed itself must list the full price, both mailing addresses and a forwarding address for the next tax bill (KRS 382.135), or the clerk cannot file it. If you are inheriting or selling an estate property, ask the clerk what extra paperwork the personal representative needs.

sections.h2: Selling an Owen County house with taxes owed
sections.html:
An open tax balance does not stop a sale. It does need to be cleared, and the order matters.

  1. Phone the sheriff for the current bill, or the clerk once April 15 has gone by.
  2. Ask for the payoff in writing, with the date it stays good through.
  3. Pass the figure to your closing agent so it can be paid out of the proceeds.
  4. Check afterward that the clerk has recorded a release.

A cash buyer can close without waiting on a bank appraisal, which helps when a house has deferred repairs or a long tax history, though the payoff is still due at closing. A clean tax record is one thing a seller fully controls, whatever the market does.

sections.h2: Questions to settle before you accept an offer
sections.html:
Before you sign a contract, answer three questions. Who paid this year's bill, and when? Is anything recorded against the parcel at the County Clerk's office? Does the deed carry an address where the buyer wants the next bill sent? None takes long, and together they remove most of the surprises that slow a closing.

If a buyer asks about the tax bill, point to the printed statement and the sheriff's phone number rather than guessing. For an inherited house, bring the paperwork that shows who has authority to sign.

faqs.q: Which office decides what my Owen County property is worth?
faqs.a: The Property Valuation Administration, 502-484-5172. Collection is the sheriff's job, valuation is not.

faqs.q: Where is the Owen County tax office?
faqs.a: In the sheriff's office at 103 W. Perry St., Owenton (502-484-3363), Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

faqs.q: Who pays transfer tax on an Owen County sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays it, at 50 cents per $500 of value with partial blocks counted whole. The clerk wants proof of payment before accepting the deed.

faqs.q: What if my bill is still open after April 15?
faqs.a: Phone the County Clerk, 502-484-2213. The bill has become a certificate of delinquency, with a lien and monthly interest of 1 percent.

faqs.q: Is a homestead exemption available in Owen County?
faqs.a: Yes, through the PVA, for residents who are 65 or older or totally disabled. Whoever buys the house applies separately.
